techniques.name: Traditional method
techniques.summary: The traditional method makes a sparkling wine by a second fermentation in the very bottle the guest is poured from. A still base wine is bottled with sugar and yeast, sealed with a crown cap and left to referment, which traps carbon dioxide as fine bubbles. The wine then rests on its dead yeast, gaining texture and notes of bread, brioche and toast, before the yeast is riddled into the neck, frozen and removed. A final dosage sets the sweetness. Champagne, Cava, Crémant, Franciacorta and English sparkling wine are all made this way.
techniques.how: Grapes are picked early for acidity and pressed gently, whole bunches in Champagne, so the juice stays pale even from black grapes. Each parcel is fermented to a dry, high acid base wine, and the cellar master blends the base wines, often with reserve wines from earlier years, into the cuvée. The liqueur de tirage, wine with sugar, selected yeast and a riddling aid, is added and the wine is bottled under a crown cap. The second fermentation, the prise de mousse, raises the alcohol by little more than a degree and builds a pressure of five to six atmospheres. The bottles then lie on their lees for months or years while the yeast breaks down. Riddling, by hand on a pupitre or by a gyropalette, works the sediment into the neck; the neck is frozen, the cap is lifted and the plug of ice and yeast shoots out. The liqueur d'expédition tops the bottle up, the cork and wire cage go on, and the wine rests again before release.
steps: Base wine
An early picked, gently pressed juice fermented dry in tank or barrel, usually through malolactic conversion.
Assemblage
Base wines from different villages, grapes and years blended into one cuvée with a house style.
Tirage
The blend bottled with sugar, yeast and a riddling aid under a crown cap.
Prise de mousse
The second fermentation in the bottle, which makes the bubbles and adds a little alcohol.
Ageing on the lees
Months or years on the dead yeast, which gives texture, a finer mousse and bready notes.
Riddling
The bottles turned and tilted, by hand or machine, until the sediment rests in the neck.
Disgorging
The neck frozen in brine, the cap removed and the plug of yeast expelled by the pressure.
Dosage
A liqueur of wine and sugar added to set the sweetness, from none at all to sweet.
techniques.why: The second fermentation in a closed bottle dissolves the carbon dioxide into the wine under pressure, so the mousse is fine and lasting. Long contact with the lees brings autolysis: the dead yeast releases compounds that add body, a creamy texture and notes of brioche, biscuit and toast, and protect the wine from oxygen. The method keeps the base wine's acidity and lets a blend show its place and its house style over many years.
techniques.law: The European Union reserves the term méthode champenoise for Champagne, so other wines made this way say méthode traditionnelle, metodo classico or método tradicional. Each appellation sets its own minimum time on the lees, and Champagne asks more than Cava, Crémant or most rules elsewhere. The dosage terms on the label, from Brut Nature to Doux, are fixed by European law and apply to every sparkling wine sold in the Union.
where: The model: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, at least fifteen months from tirage for a non-vintage wine.
Cava, mostly from Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada, aged at least nine months on its lees.
Franciacorta, from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with longer minimum ageing on the lees than Champagne for its non-vintage wine.
Sparkling wines from the Champagne grapes on chalk and greensand in the south of the country.
Crémant de Loire and Saumur, often from Chenin Blanc.

deeper.head: Minimum time on the lees
deeper.text: Champagne asks at least 15 months from tirage before release for a non-vintage wine, 12 of them on the lees, and at least three years for a vintage wine. Cava asks at least nine months on its lees, with longer minimums for Reserva and Gran Reserva, and Crémant asks nine. Franciacorta asks 18 months on the lees for its non-vintage wine.

deeper.head: The transfer method
deeper.text: Some houses ferment in bottle and then empty the bottles into a pressurised tank, filter out the lees and rebottle the wine. The wine keeps the texture of a bottle fermentation without riddling or disgorging each bottle. In the United States such a wine may be labelled bottle fermented, while a wine of the traditional method itself can say fermented in this bottle.

deeper.head: Autolysis and the age of the lees
deeper.text: Autolysis begins only after several months on the lees, as the yeast cell walls break down and release mannoproteins, amino acids and other compounds. The mannoproteins help the wine hold its carbon dioxide and give a finer, creamier mousse, while the amino acids feed the slow reactions that bring brioche, biscuit and nutty notes. That is why long ageing before disgorgement, rather than after it, is prized.

A candidate is asked to tie each dosage term to its range in grams per litre: Brut Nature under 3 with no sugar added, Extra Brut up to 6, Brut under 12, Extra Dry 12 to 17, Sec 17 to 32, Demi-Sec 32 to 50 and Doux above 50. The overlaps let one wine qualify for two terms.

exam: Name the eight steps in order, from base wine to dosage.
Know the minimum lees ageing for Champagne, Cava, Crémant and Franciacorta.
Know the dosage terms and their sweetness, Brut Nature to Doux.
Explain what autolysis gives a sparkling wine.
traps: Méthode champenoise may not appear on a label outside Champagne within the European Union.
Bottle fermented on an American label can mean the transfer method, not riddling and disgorging.
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, not drier.
The tank method also makes a second fermentation, but in a sealed tank, not the bottle.

cards.f: Traditional method: where does the second fermentation happen?
cards.b: In the bottle the wine is sold in, after the tirage adds sugar and yeast to the base wine.

cards.f: Liqueur de tirage: what is in it?
cards.b: Wine, sugar, selected yeast and a riddling aid, added to the base wine before it is bottled under a crown cap.

cards.f: Prise de mousse: what is it?
cards.b: The second fermentation in the bottle, which makes the bubbles and raises the alcohol by little more than a degree.
Turns and tilts the bottle, on a pupitre or a gyropalette, until the yeast sediment rests in the neck.

cards.f: Disgorging: how is the yeast removed?
cards.b: The neck is frozen, the crown cap lifted, and the pressure expels the plug of ice and yeast.
The sweetness, through the liqueur d'expédition added after disgorging, from Brut Nature to Doux.

cards.f: Autolysis: what does it give the wine?
cards.b: Body, a creamy mousse and notes of brioche, biscuit and toast, from the dead yeast breaking down over months on the lees.

cards.f: Champagne non-vintage: minimum time before release?
cards.b: Fifteen months from tirage, twelve of them on the lees.

cards.f: Transfer method: how does it differ?
cards.b: The wine ferments in bottle but is emptied into a tank, filtered and rebottled, so nothing is riddled or disgorged.

questions.q: Where does the second fermentation of a traditional method wine take place?
opts: In the bottle it is sold in
questions.exp: The tirage starts a second fermentation in the bottle itself, which traps the carbon dioxide; the tank method referments in a sealed tank instead.

questions.q: What is the French name for the second fermentation in the bottle?
questions.exp: The prise de mousse is the second fermentation; dégorgement removes the yeast, assemblage is the blend and the liqueur de tirage starts the fermentation.

questions.q: Which dosage term on a sparkling wine label means the sweetest wine of these four?
questions.exp: Extra Dry holds 12 to 17 grams of sugar per litre, sweeter than Brut; Extra Brut and Brut Nature are drier still.

questions.q: What is the process called in which dead yeast breaks down and gives a sparkling wine notes of brioche?
questions.exp: Autolysis, after months on the lees, releases compounds that give body, a creamy mousse and bready, toasty notes.

questions.q: What is the minimum time from tirage before a non-vintage Champagne may be released?
questions.exp: Non-vintage Champagne needs fifteen months from tirage, twelve on the lees; nine months is the Cava and Crémant minimum, thirty-six the vintage rule.

questions.q: Which method ferments in bottle but then empties the wine into a tank to filter and rebottle it?
questions.exp: The transfer method keeps the texture of a bottle fermentation but skips riddling and disgorging each bottle; American labels may call it bottle fermented.

techniques.name: Carbonic maceration
techniques.summary: Carbonic maceration ferments whole, uncrushed bunches of red grapes in a vessel filled with carbon dioxide. Without oxygen, each berry begins to ferment inside its own skin, an enzyme reaction that makes a little alcohol, softens the acidity and draws colour from the skins with little tannin. The grapes are then pressed and yeast finishes the fermentation. The wines are bright and fruity, with notes of kirsch, banana and bubblegum, soft tannin and an early peak: Beaujolais Nouveau is the model.
techniques.how: The grapes must reach the winery as whole, unbroken bunches, which is why they are picked by hand. They are tipped into a closed vat that is filled with carbon dioxide, or that fills itself as the bottom of the vat ferments. Inside each intact berry, enzymes turn some sugar into alcohol and break down some malic acid, while colour and aroma move from the skins into the pulp. After one to three weeks the free run wine is drawn off, the grapes are pressed, and yeast finishes the fermentation of the juice to dryness, usually away from the skins. In semi-carbonic maceration, the common Beaujolais form, the weight of the bunches crushes the grapes at the bottom, whose juice ferments with yeast and gives off the gas that blankets the rest.
steps: Hand harvest
Whole bunches arrive unbroken so the berries stay intact.
Filling the vat
Bunches go into a closed vat under a blanket of carbon dioxide.
Intracellular fermentation
Enzymes inside each berry make a little alcohol and soften the acidity without yeast.
Pressing
After days or weeks the free run wine is drawn off and the grapes are pressed.
Yeast fermentation
The juice finishes fermenting to dryness, usually off the skins.
techniques.why: The method draws colour and fruit from the skins with little tannin, and the enzyme reaction makes aromas of kirsch, banana, bubblegum and cinnamon. Malic acid falls, so the wine feels soft. The result is a red to drink young and lightly chilled, for the fruit fades within a few years.
techniques.law: No law requires carbonic maceration, but the Beaujolais appellations require hand harvesting, which keeps the whole bunches the method needs. Beaujolais Nouveau, the first wine of the vintage, may be released only from the third Thursday of November.
where: Gamay in semi-carbonic maceration, from Beaujolais Nouveau to the crus, where it is often shortened for structure.
Carignan from old vines, softened by carbonic maceration in Corbières and Minervois.
The young cosechero reds of Rioja Alavesa, fermented in whole bunches by tradition.

deeper.head: Semi-carbonic and full carbonic
deeper.text: Full carbonic maceration seals intact bunches under carbon dioxide from the start, so nearly every berry ferments within its skin. Semi-carbonic, the Beaujolais way, simply fills the vat with bunches: the crushed fruit at the bottom ferments with yeast and its gas protects the whole berries above. Many producers of the Beaujolais crus shorten the maceration and press sooner, for a wine with more structure.

deeper.head: What the berry makes on its own
deeper.text: Inside the intact berry, without yeast, enzymes convert a small share of the sugar to alcohol, commonly about 2 per cent by volume, and break down a good part of the malic acid. The reaction also makes the esters behind the banana and bubblegum notes, chiefly isoamyl acetate, and lets anthocyanins move into the pulp while little tannin is extracted.

deeper.head: Nouveau and the release date
deeper.text: Beaujolais Nouveau is a vin de primeur, sold from the third Thursday of November of its own vintage, a date set in 1985. Most Nouveau is made by short semi-carbonic maceration, and the appellation rules that require hand harvesting keep the whole bunches the method needs.

Beyond Beaujolais, whole bunch carbonic fermentation softens Carignan and Syrah in the Languedoc and shapes the young cosechero reds of Rioja Alavesa; many natural wine producers now use it for light, chillable reds from Gamay, Pinot Noir and other grapes.

exam: Describe intracellular fermentation and what it gives the wine.
Tie semi-carbonic maceration to Gamay and Beaujolais.
Know the release date of Beaujolais Nouveau.
traps: Carbonic maceration needs intact berries under carbon dioxide; whole bunch fermentation in an open vat is a different technique.
The banana note comes from isoamyl acetate, not from the Gamay grape itself.
Many Beaujolais crus use little or no carbonic maceration and age for years.

cards.f: Carbonic maceration: what goes into the vat?
cards.b: Whole, uncrushed bunches of red grapes, under a blanket of carbon dioxide.
Enzymes inside each intact berry turn some sugar into alcohol and break down malic acid, without yeast.

cards.f: Carbonic maceration: the aromas it gives
cards.b: Kirsch, banana, bubblegum and cinnamon, with bright red fruit.

cards.f: Carbonic maceration: the structure it gives
cards.b: Deep colour with little tannin and soft acidity, a wine to drink young.

cards.f: Carbonic maceration: why pick by hand?
cards.b: The berries must stay whole and unbroken for the fermentation inside each one.

cards.f: Carbonic maceration: the classic region and grape
cards.b: Beaujolais and Gamay, usually in the semi-carbonic form.

cards.f: Semi-carbonic maceration: how does it work?
cards.b: Bunches fill the vat, the bottom grapes are crushed and ferment with yeast, and their gas blankets the whole berries above.

cards.f: Carbonic maceration: the ester behind the banana note

questions.q: What fills the vat in carbonic maceration before the whole bunches ferment?
questions.exp: Carbon dioxide excludes oxygen, so each intact berry begins an enzyme fermentation inside its own skin.

questions.q: Which grape is most associated with carbonic maceration in Beaujolais?
questions.exp: Gamay is the grape of Beaujolais, made mostly by semi-carbonic maceration; Carignan is softened this way in the Languedoc.

questions.q: Which aroma is typical of a young wine made by carbonic maceration?
questions.exp: Carbonic maceration makes isoamyl acetate, the ester behind banana and bubblegum; petrol marks aged Riesling, toast comes from oak or lees, leather from age.

questions.q: What is the fermentation inside each intact berry, without yeast, called?
questions.exp: Intracellular fermentation is the enzyme reaction inside the unbroken berry that makes a little alcohol and softens the acidity.

questions.q: On which day may Beaujolais Nouveau first be released?
questions.exp: Beaujolais Nouveau is released from the third Thursday of November of its vintage, a date fixed in 1985.

questions.q: Which ester gives carbonic maceration wines their banana note?
questions.exp: Isoamyl acetate, made in quantity during carbonic maceration, gives the banana and bubblegum notes of young Beaujolais.
